extracted.intended_audience: pragmatics scholars, linguists, and students studying humor and relevance theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing or designing verbal jokes using Sperber & Wilson's Relevance Theory as extended by Francisco Yus — focusing on accessibility rankings, garden‑pathing, and weakly communicated implicatures as sources of humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance-theoretic communicative premise
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary communication, the hearer (1) makes hypotheses about the speaker's intended meaning, (2) selects the most accessible interpretation that yields enough cognitive effects for the processing effort, and (3) stops when an optimally relevant interpretation is found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational model Yus assumes: the hearer's inferential strategy (seeking an optimally relevant interpretation) is what speakers can manipulate to produce humour. Use this model to explain why certain interpretive paths are taken and where manipulation can occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garden-path joke structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes exploit the hearer's default strategy by priming a high-accessibility interpretation A, leading the hearer to commit to A, then using a punchline incompatible with A to force selection of a lower-accessibility interpretation B that was supported but not reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yus's canonical five-step sequence: (1) setup primes interpretation A; (2) hearer commits to A; (3) punchline incompatible with A; (4) punch forces low-accessibility B; (5) reinterpretation under B yields the joke effect. When evaluating or creating garden-path jokes, check that each step is present and that B was genuinely supported by the setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive overload via weakly communicated assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes produce laughter not from a single incongruity-resolution but from a cognitive overload of weakly communicated assumptions: the punchline implies many things simultaneously (about characters, situation, norms, stereotypes) and the proliferation of weak implicatures is itself the source of comic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess jokes for the density of weak implicatures: deeper jokes have many resonances; translations often lose force because those assumptions fail to carry; insider jokes are funnier to insiders because more weak assumptions are accessible. For production, design punchlines that trigger a halo of weak implications rather than a single neat reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 1 — Single-covert interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: One interpretation A is salient throughout; the punchline reveals interpretation B that was always available but covert; the hearer realizes B fits all along.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether B was genuinely available from the setup (covert but supported) and whether the reveal makes the prior text cohere under B. This type is the prototypical incongruity-resolution structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 2 — Multi-graded interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Several interpretations are simultaneously available and ranked by accessibility; the punchline reveals that a low-ranked interpretation is intended, producing pleasure from being made to traverse the ranking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for a clear accessibility ranking in the setup and for the punchline to force re-ranking or movement to a less accessible reading. The comic effect relies on the perceptible journey across multiple candidate interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 3 — Weakly-implicated propositions (halo of meanings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline does not yield a single intended interpretation but a halo of weak implications; the hearer enjoys the spread of meanings. Ironic and rich literary humor often takes this form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the multiplicity and subtlety of implicatures evoked by the punchline. This type emphasizes breadth and resonance over a single tight twist; measure 'depth' by how many weak implicatures are plausibly activated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition: setup primes A without requiring it
rubrics_metrics.description: The setup makes interpretation A maximally accessible without requiring it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a successful relevance-theoretic joke, the setup should bias the hearer strongly toward A while still leaving B (or other readings) linguistically possible. If A is required (not just accessible), the punch cannot retroactively reassign interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition: B is genuinely supported but less accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation B must be genuinely supported by the linguistic content of the setup but be less accessible than A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a joke, verify that B isn't ad hoc or purely inferentially invented by the punchline; B should have evidential support in the setup even if low in accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition: punchline blocks A and/or triggers weak assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline must block A and force B, or the punchline must trigger a cloud of weak assumptions (the weak-implicature route).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between a punchline that performs an overturning (blocking A) and one that proliferates weak implicatures; both can produce humour but operate differently. Evaluate which mechanism is at work to explain the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary condition: hearer recognizes speaker's manipulation (intentionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hearer must recognize the speaker's manipulation — the joke depends on attributing intentional design to the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the hearer models the speaker as having deliberately constructed the misleading path. If the re-interpretation is perceived as a mere coincidence or accident, it will not produce the same relevance-theoretic humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker intentionality as a humour requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A spontaneous coincidence is not funny in the same way as an intentional joke; relevance-theoretic humour requires that the hearer model that the speaker deliberately constructed the misleading path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion when explaining differences between accidental oddities and jokes: intentional design converts interpretive surprise into a 'victory' of speaker over hearer's ordinary processing and thus into humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of questions to diagnose the joke's interpretive structure: What is the most accessible interpretation A from the setup? What is the alternative interpretation B that the punchline forces? Is the punchline blocking A and forcing B, or is it spreading weak assumptions? Does the hearer model the speaker's design (intentional manipulation)? Are there many weak implicatures supporting 'depth,' or just one twist?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these questions when analyzing or constructing jokes to determine type (single-covert, multi-graded, weakly-implicated), mechanism (blocking vs. proliferation), and whether necessary conditions are met. They also serve as a checklist for why a joke may fail (e.g., B unsupported, no perceived intent, too few implicatures).
